ety.text: Ancient Greek ῥῠθμός (rhŭthmós)bor. Latin rhythmusder. English rhythm First coined in 1557, from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós, “any measured flow or movement, symmetry, rhythm”), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, run, stream, gush”).

senses.d: The variation of strong and weak elements (such as duration, accent) of sounds, notably in speech or music, over time; a beat or meter.
ex: Dance to the rhythm of the music.
The audience clapped in rhythm as I sang.

senses.d: A specifically defined pattern of such variation.
ex: Most dances have a rhythm as distinctive as the Iambic verse in poetry

senses.d: A flow, repetition or regularity.
ex: Once you get the rhythm of it, the job will become easy.

senses.d: The tempo or speed of a beat, song or repetitive event.
ex: We walked with a quick, even rhythm.
Bigeminous rhythm was followed by bursts of extrasystoles.

senses.d: The musical instruments which provide rhythm (mainly; not or less melody) in a musical ensemble.
ex: The Baroque term basso continuo is virtually equivalent to rhythm

senses.d: A regular quantitative change in a variable (notably natural) process.
ex: The rhythm of the seasons dominates agriculture as well as wildlife

senses.d: Controlled repetition of a phrase, incident or other element as a stylistic figure in literature and other narrative arts; the effect it creates.
ex: The running gag is a popular rhythm in motion pictures and theater comedy

senses.d: A person's natural feeling for rhythm.
ex: That girl's got rhythm, watch her dance!
I'm never gonna dance again / Guilty feet have got no rhythm

senses.d: To impart a (particular) rhythm to.

grp.label: variation of strong and weak elements of sounds over time
tempo or speed of a beat, song, or repeated event

From Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

From Middle English rim, rime, ryme (“identical letters or sounds in words from the vowel in their stressed syllables to their ends; measure, meter, rhythm; song, verse, etc., with rhyming lines”), from Anglo-Norman rime, ryme (“identical letters or sounds in words from the vowel in their stressed syllables to their ends; song, verse, etc., with rhyming lines”) (modern French rime); further etymology uncertain, possibly either: * from Latin rhythmus (“rhythm”), from Ancient Greek ῥῠθμός (rhŭthmós, “measured motion, rhythm; regular, repeating motion, vibration”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Euro…

chain.g: to rhyme (a word) with another word; to write verse

ety.text: From Middle English rimen, rymen, rim, rime (“to recite or write verse; to sing songs; to tell a story in verse; to fit into verse; (figurative) to agree, make sense”), from Anglo-Norman rimer, Middle French rimer, and Old French rimer (“to rhyme (a word) with another word; to write verse”) (modern French rimer), Old French rime, ryme (noun): see etymology 1.

senses.d: Rhyming verse (poetic form).
ex: Many editors say they don’t want stories written in rhyme these days.
Libels are caſt againſt thee in the ſtreete, / Ballads and rimes made of thy ouerthrovv.

senses.d: A thought expressed in verse; a verse; a poem; a tale told in verse.
ex: Tennyson’s rhymes

senses.d: A word that rhymes with another.
ex: Norse poetry is littered with rhymes like “sól … sunnan”.
Rap makes use of rhymes such as “money … honey” and “nope … dope”.

senses.d: A word that rhymes with another, in that it is pronounced identically with the other word from the vowel in its stressed syllable to the end.
ex: "Awake" is a rhyme for "lake".

senses.d: Rhyming: sameness of letters or sounds of part of some words.
ex: The poem exhibits a peculiar form of rhyme.

senses.d: The second part of a syllable, from the vowel on, as opposed to the onset.
An instance of rapping; a rapped verse; a line or couple lines of rapping; a hip hop song.
ex: I heard Drake's new rhyme last night.

senses.d: A rapper's oeuvre, lyricism or skill.
ex: His rhymes are all weak.

senses.d: Number.
To compose or treat in verse; versify.
ex: Ha, ha, hovv vildely doth this Cynicke rime?
How Panurge and the rest rim'd with Poetick Fury [chapter title]

senses.d: To place (a word or words) in such a way as to produce a rhyme or an approximation thereof.
ex:
Now she's tainted by the syringe
Try to rhyme a word with orange

senses.d: Of a word, to be pronounced identically with another from the vowel in its stressed syllable to the end.
ex: Creation rhymes with integration and station.
India and windier rhyme with each other in non-rhotic accents.

senses.d: To be pronounced identically from the vowel in the stressed syllable of each to the end of each.
ex: Mug and rug rhyme.

senses.d: To contain words that are pronounced identically to each other from the vowel in the stressed syllable to the end.
ex: I rewrote the story to make it rhyme.

senses.d: To somewhat resemble or correspond with.
To number; count; reckon.

grp.label: rhyming; sameness of letters or sounds of some parts of words, as ‘the poem exhibits rhyme’
